A1.justification: Both PDFs describe DEFT. Their complete main texts and Appendices A.1–A.9, including figures, tables, equations, and algorithms, are readable and support comparison despite reflow and additions.

before.justification: v3 reports original latency, IO, GPU-utilization, and numerical-accuracy experiments across three decoding workloads, including extensive appendix results.

after.justification: v4 retains original empirical evaluations, revises several measurements, and adds the speculative-decoding prompt-length experiments in Figures 16–18.

M1.justification: KV-guided grouping, flattened KV splitting, bit masks, and tree-aware reduction remain unchanged. Algorithms 1–4 and their accompanying explanations are identical after accounting for pagination; the redesigned Figure 3 illustrates the existing procedure.

E1.justification: The APPS workloads and four GoT reasoning tasks remain. Appendix A.7 adds an explicit long-prompt, short-generation speculative-decoding scenario, extending prompts to 20,000 tokens with 1,000 generated tokens. This expands tested input conditions without introducing another dataset or core task.

E2.justification: Figure 4 adds DEFT-Node-Chunk to the existing latency-breakdown comparison, although this variant was already evaluated elsewhere in v3. The main external baseline set remains Flash-Decoding, Tree Attention-Medusa, and Radix Attention; newly cited concurrent methods are not empirically added.

E3.justification: Section 4.3 revises the reported timing metric from end-to-end to decoding latency, explicitly excluding prefill and framework overheads; this does not establish that retained experiments were rerun. The new appendix protocol uses Llama3.1-8B on A100 80GB, prompts of 1,000–20,000 tokens, fixed 1,000-token generation, tree sizes 32/64, and time per output token alongside decoding and attention latency.

E4.justification: Figures 16–18 add prompt-length sensitivity tests comparing Radix Attention and three DEFT variants in speculative decoding. Figure 4 extends the component-overhead analysis to DEFT-Node-Chunk. Existing tree-width, chunk-size, GPU, model-size, and numerical-accuracy analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version provides repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance testing for the performance results. Figure 13's unchanged standard deviation describes variation in tree-node lengths, not experimental uncertainty.

E6.justification: Central speculative-decoding results change substantially in Tables 5, 6, and 16. At tree size 256, Table 16 replaces DEFT-Flatten/Radix attention latencies of 55.58/212.29 seconds with 40.56/145.43 seconds, changing the reported speedup from 3.82× to 3.59×. Table 5's maximum reported speedup changes from 2.52× end-to-end to 2.23× decoding. Table 6 reverses the Node versus Node-Chunk ordering at size 128. Figure 4's measurements are revised, Figures 16–18 add results, and Table 1 corrects 94.61 to 94.67 seconds. These changes do not establish same-protocol performance gains.

T1.justification: Equation 1, the segmented-attention reasoning in Appendix A.3, and the IO definitions and complexity analysis in Tables 11–12 remain unchanged. The expanded Figure 11 caption explains an already illustrated bit mask without adding a mathematical result.

C1.justification: The algorithmic contributions and three-workload effectiveness claim remain. The abstract, introduction, and conclusion narrow the quantitative acceleration claim: the headline changes from up to 2.52× end-to-end and 3.82× attention speedup to 2.23× decoding and 3.59× attention speedup.

C2.justification: Section 4.3 newly qualifies decoding latency as excluding prefill, estimated at 5–10% of end-to-end latency, and framework overheads, estimated at 10–15%, justifying exclusion as consistent across baselines. Appendix A.7 and Table 16 also explicitly distinguish attention latency from KV-management overhead. These qualifications clarify the practical scope of the efficiency claims.

D1.justification: v4 adds a project repository link and code-availability statement. Table 4 newly specifies padding few-shot prompts to 4,000 tokens and approximately 3,500 reasoning iterations. Since v3 already states a 4,000-token prompt, the padding disclosure alone does not establish changed preprocessing.

R1.justification: v4 adds Cascade Inference and RelayAttention to the references and concurrent-work discussion. Section 2 and Appendix A.3 position them alongside shared-prefix approaches, with Table 9's caption relating them to Hydragen. The broader research positioning remains unchanged.

P1.justification: The section hierarchy and most prose remain intact. Edits concentrate on decoding-latency terminology, a revised Section 4.3 explanation, expanded figure captions, publication and corresponding-author information, and a new acknowledgement.

P2.justification: Figure 3 is substantially reorganized into three panels explaining dataflow, grouping, and flattened splitting. Figure 4 gains another method bar, a revised legend order, and a rescaled latency axis. Figures 16–18 introduce paired sensitivity plots, while Table 1 and Tables 7–8 are repositioned. These materially revise the visual explanation and experimental presentation; retained appendix plots and algorithms are matched across moves.

improvement.justification: v4 improves transparency by explicitly separating decoding measurements from full end-to-end latency. The additional prompt-length analysis, clearer Figure 3, and code-access information provide useful support for the unchanged method. Several revised latency values lack an explanation connecting the old and new measurements, limiting confidence in interpreting those replacements. Overall, the documentation and supporting-analysis gains constitute a limited improvement.
